terms.comment: To throw someone into prison, in carcerem conjicere (Traupman 196) or compingere (Plaut. Amph. 155). In the plural, carcerēs are also the starting gates of a race.
in vincula conjicere, to put in irons, to imprison (Caes.; Liv.).
To take into custody, in custōdiam trādere (Liv. 22.52); to be held in custody, in custōdiā habērī (Traupman 194).
Lewis & Short knows it only from an inscription; the classical jailer is the custōs or carcerārius (Plaut.).

phrases.latin: quid faciam nunc, sī trēs virī mē in carcerem compēgerint?
phrases.english: what am I to do now, if the night magistrates lock me up in jail?

phrases.latin: esse carcerem, quem vindicem nefāriōrum ac manifestōrum scelerum majōrēs nostrī esse voluērunt
phrases.english: that there is a prison, which our ancestors meant to be the avenger of wicked and flagrant crimes

phrases.source: Traupman 196; cf. Cic. Verr. 2.5.17 (Lewis & Short s.v. conjiciō)

phrases.english: to lock someone up in prison
phrases.source: Traupman 196; cf. Plaut. Am. 1.1.3 (Lewis & Short s.v. compingō)

phrases.english: to haul someone off to prison
to sentence someone to life imprisonment

phrases.source: Traupman 195; cf. Liv. 24.45.8: lībera, private custody (Lewis & Short s.v. custōdia)

phrases.english: They will soon be sitting in jail.

phrases.source: Liv. 24.45.8 (Lewis & Short s.v. custōdia: private custody, confinement in one’s house); Traupman 330
